data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["A map is a spatial representation; a checklist is a procedural one.","A map's validity is geographically fixed; a checklist's validity may depend on the user's execution."],"overturn_conditions":["The checklist incorporates mechanisms for handling uncertainty or novel cases, bridging the gap between proxy and model.","The non-expert panel's error patterns are demonstrably different from the checklist's theoretical failure modes, suggesting emergent understanding."],"shared_structure":["Both involve a proxy (map/checklist) for a reality (territory/expert knowledge).","Both can be perfectly useful and 'correct' within their domain of validity.","Both conflate the proxy with the reality at their peril."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_008","SRC_002"],"transfer_claims":["The 'proxy' transfer: a checklist that works is not a sign of genuine understanding, but of a valid proxy. The danger is when the proxy fails and the user has no deeper model to fall back on.","The underdetermination thesis: within a single evaluation (a single trip with the map), you cannot tell if the map is perfect or if you just got lucky."]},"claim":"A trained non-expert panel will not reliably outperform an expert because tacit knowledge, essential for many verifiable-outcome tasks, cannot be fully externalized into an explicit checklist. The distinction between genuine reliability and mere compliance is impossible to draw from a single evaluation because the panel's success on the evaluated items may be entirely due to the checklist having encoded the expert's tacit knowledge into a set of proxy rules that happen to work on that specific case-set.
